abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is a major risk factor for anxiety, depression and substance use disorders later in life, and it is thought to act in part by changing how emotion-regulating circuits develop. The prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices exert top-down control over the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and this circuit is still maturing during early postnatal life. Stress in adulthood removes dendritic spines from prefrontal neurons, but it is less clear whether ELS causes lasting spine changes across this circuit, and the IL in particular has rarely been studied. Here, we asked whether ELS alters dendritic spine density in the PL, IL and BLA of adult male mice. From postnatal day (PND) 10 to 17, ELS pups were separated from the dam for 3 h per day and individually isolated from their littermates, and their home cage had reduced nesting material until PND21. Control pups were separated together with their littermates for only 15 min per day and kept standard nesting. In adulthood, brains were processed for Golgi-Cox staining, and spines were counted on proximal apical and basal dendrites of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the PL and IL, and on dendrites of principal neurons in the BLA. ELS reduced spine density by approximately 30% in the IL and PL dendrites, with the largest losses concentrated on proximal apical dendrites. The BLA showed a smaller reduction of about 12%. These preliminary findings suggest that ELS leads to an important and lasting loss of dendritic spines in prefrontal regions that regulate emotional responses.
